Stepping into politics after the death of her husband, three-time president Arnulfo Arias, she became this Central American nation's first — and so far only — female president, serving from 1999 to 2004. Who is she?
Mireya Moscoso: President of Panama from 1999 to 2004. Mireya Elisa Moscoso Rodríguez (born 1 July 1946) is a Panamanian politician who served as the President of Panama from 1999 to 2004.

Avenging the slain Husayn at Karbala, this pro-Alid revolutionary led a rebellion from Kufa against the Umayyads in 685 and ruled most of Iraq for eighteen months during the Second Fitna — who was he?

This South African anti-apartheid activist spent his revolutionary decades fighting to dismantle racial oppression, became the nation's first Black president in 1994, and spent his administration fostering reconciliation and building multiracial democracy. Who was he?
Nelson Mandela: President of South Africa from 1994 to 1999.
Known as 'Light of the Faith,' this Zengid dynasty ruler governed Seljuk Syria from 1146 to 1174 and looms large in the history of the Second Crusade — who was he?
Nur al-Din Zengi: Emir of Aleppo (1146–1174) and Damascus (1154–1174)
The first prime minister of India from the south, he steered the country's 1991 economic liberalisation after previously serving as chief minister of Andhra Pradesh — who is he?
P. V. Narasimha Rao: Prime Minister of India from 1991 to 1996.
A four-star general who staged a 1999 coup against Nawaz Sharif's government, this military officer went on to serve as Pakistan's president from 2001 to 2008 — who was he?

Pervez Musharraf: President of Pakistan from 2001 to 2008. Pervez Musharraf (11 August 1943 – 5 February 2023) was a Pakistani politician and military officer who served as the tenth president of Pakistan from 2001 to 2008.
This act of deliberate communication with a deity — through hymns, incantations, or spontaneous words — has been documented in written sources for some five thousand years — what is it called?
Prayer: Invocation or act that seeks to activate a rapport with a deity.
His 1965 book Unsafe at Any Speed lambasted the auto industry's safety record and helped spur a landmark 1966 vehicle-safety law; he later ran for president — which consumer crusader is he?
Ralph Nader: American lawyer and activist (born 1934)
Forced to resign from the hospital company he co-founded after it pleaded guilty to defrauding Medicare, this businessman later became the 45th governor of Florida — who is he?
Tradition holds this Varangian chieftain was invited to reign in Novgorod in 862, founding the dynasty that ruled Russia until 1598 — who was he?
Rurik: Varangian chieftain of the Rus'. The Primary Chronicle states that Rurik was succeeded by his kinsman Oleg who was regent for his infant son Igor.
A former partisan and socialist politician, this journalist-turned-statesman served as president of Italy from 1978 to 1985 — who is he?
Sandro Pertini: President of Italy from 1978 to 1985.
At 35, he became Russia's youngest-ever prime minister in 1998 and later ran the Rosatom nuclear agency for over a decade — who is this Kremlin technocrat?
Sergey Kiriyenko: Prime Minister of Russia In 1998.
A Jagiellonian king of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1506, he earned his "the Old" nickname only later, to tell him apart from the son who succeeded him. Who was this monarch?
Sigismund I the Old: King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1506 to 1548. Sigismund was born in the town of Kozienice in 1467 as the fifth son of Casimir IV and Elizabeth of Austria.
Crowned in 1576 after marrying Queen Anna Jagiellon, this ruler defeated a rival claimant to become the third elected king of Poland — who was he?
Stephen Báthory: Ruler of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth from 1576 to 1586.
Born in Doha in 1980, this man only became heir after an older brother renounced the throne — and he's reigned over his Gulf nation since 2013. Who is he?
Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani: Emir of Qatar since 2013.

This South Australian premier governed for over 26 years — the longest unbroken stretch of any elected leader in Australian history — and was famous for shamelessly haranguing federal leaders into funding his state. Who was he?
Thomas Playford IV: 20th-century Australian politician and fruit grower (1896–1981)
This self-proclaimed Sapa Inca led a large Andean rebellion against Spanish colonial rule in Peru and later became a symbol of the independence movement — who was he?
Túpac Amaru II: Leader of an uprising in Peru.

His name became a byword for traitor, but this Norwegian officer once worked alongside explorer Fridtjof Nansen on famine relief before heading the Nazi puppet government during Germany's occupation of Norway — who is it?
Vidkun Quisling: Norwegian politician and Nazi collaborator (1887–1945)

In 1806, fearing Napoleon's growing power after the Confederation of the Rhine formed, Prussia joined Russia, Saxony, Sweden and Britain in a fresh multinational stand against the French Empire — which conflict?
War of the Fourth Coalition: 1806–1807 conflict of the Napoleonic Wars.
It's the season that arrives when your hemisphere tilts away from the Sun, so that while one half of Earth shivers the other basks in summer. Which season?
Winter: Coldest of the four temperate seasons.
He ran the KGB for 15 years before briefly becoming the Soviet Union's General Secretary in 1982 — and decades earlier, as ambassador to Hungary, helped crush its 1956 uprising. Who is he?
Yuri Andropov: Leader of the Soviet Union from 1982 to 1984.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Zhuge Liang (born 181) is the earliest of the four. After helping found Shu Han, Zhuge Liang exercised near-total authority over both civil and military affairs.
Which of these people was born first?
Ma Jun (mechanical engineer) (born 200) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Zhuge Liang (born 181) is the earliest of the four. After helping found Shu Han, Zhuge Liang exercised near-total authority over both civil and military affairs.
Which of these four is the oldest?
Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the astronomer from these four.
Fritz Zwicky is an astronomer. Fritz Zwicky (German: [ˈtsvɪki]; February 14, 1898 – February 8, 1974) was a Swiss astronomer.
Which of these four is a mathematician?
What is the atomic number of Ruthenium?
Ruthenium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ru and atomic number 44.
What is the atomic number of Chlorine?
Chlorine is a chemical element; it has symbol Cl and atomic number 17.
In what year was Ernest Lawrence born?
Ernest Lawrence: A graduate of the University of South Dakota and University of Minnesota, Lawrence obtained a PhD in physics at Yale in 1925.
In what year was Richard Feynman born?
Richard Feynman: Richard Phillips Feynman (May 11, 1918 – February 15, 1988) was an American theoretical physicist.
In what year was Klaus Schwab born?
Klaus Schwab: Klaus Martin Schwab (German: [klaʊs ˈmaʁtiːn ʃvaːp]; born 30 March 1938) is a German mechanical engineer, economist, and founder of the World Economic Forum (WEF).
In what year did Saint Valentine die?
Saint Valentine was a clergyman – either a priest or a bishop – in the Roman Empire who ministered to persecuted Christians.
In what year did Niels Bohr die?
Niels Bohr: Although the Bohr model has been supplanted by other models, its underlying principles remain valid.
In what year was Benzene discovered?
Benzene is an organic chemical compound with the molecular formula C6H6.
Perl: Larry Wall. Perl is a high-level, general-purpose, interpreted, dynamic programming language.
IAI Kfir: Israel Aerospace Industries Ltd.
Which country is Beriev A-50 from?
Beriev A-50: Russia. Developed to replace the Tupolev Tu-126 "Moss", the A-50 first flew in 1978.
Who is credited with discovering Penicillin?
Penicillin: Alexander Fleming. Penicillin was discovered in 1928 by the Scottish physician Alexander Fleming as a crude extract of P. rubens.
2C-B: Alexander Shulgin. 2C-B, also known as 4-bromo-2,5-dimethoxyphenethylamine or by names such as Nexus or Erox, is a psychedelic drug of the phenethylamine and 2C families.
Who is credited with discovering Chromium?
Chromium: Louis Nicolas Vauquelin. Chromium is a chemical element; it has symbol Cr and atomic number 24.
When a message is designed to spark an immediate purchase, it's called the 'direct-response' kind of this consumer-facing practice. What is it?
Advertising is the practice and techniques employed to bring attention to a product or service.
Its type species, a common freshwater organism constantly studied in classrooms and labs, lends its name to an entire genus of shape-changing single-celled organisms — what's the genus?
Amoeba (genus) is a genus of single-celled amoeboids in the family Amoebidae.

Sitting at the milder end of a spectrum of diminished motivation — less severe than abulia and far short of akinetic mutism — this is a state marked by an absence of feeling, interest, or concern. What is it?
Apathy is a lack of feeling, emotion, interest, and/or concern about something.
This American psychologist developed the philosophy of radical behaviorism and pioneered operant conditioning while a longtime professor at Harvard — who is he?
B. F. Skinner (March 20, 1904 - August 18, 1990) was an American psychologist, behaviorist, inventor, and social philosopher.

The bassist of a legendary British rock band from 1962 to 1993, performing on its first 19 studio albums, this musician was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1989 as part of that group — who is he?
Bill Wyman (n Perks; born 24 October 1936) is an English musician who was the bassist of the rock band the Rolling Stones from 1962 to 1993.
One of the largest, longest-lived trees in the Amazon, this species produces a fruit and shell weighing up to two kilograms, with edible seeds famed for their selenium content — what tree is it?
Brazil nut (Bertholletia excelsa) refers to a South American tree of the monotypic genus Bertholletia in the family Lecythidaceae as well as the tree's commercially-harvested edible seeds.

Spread through contact with infected feces and capable of killing up to 91% of untreated cases, this highly contagious virus mainly strikes dogs and wolves but can also infect foxes, cats, and skunks — what's the virus?
Canine parvovirus (also referred to as CPV, CPV2, or parvo) is a contagious virus mainly affecting dogs and wolves.
This English polymath is credited with inventing the first mechanical computer and designing an unrealized 'analytical engine' programmed using ideas borrowed from the Jacquard loom. Who is he?
Charles Babbage (26 December 1791 - 18 October 1871) was an English polymath.
Born near Toulouse, this French inventor is remembered chiefly as an aviation pioneer — though in 1870 he was also an early enthusiast of cycling in France; who was he?
Clément Ader (French; 2 April 1841 - 3 May 1925) was a French inventor and engineer who was born near Toulouse in Muret, Haute-Garonne, and died in Toulouse.
Derived from Greek words meaning universe and study of, this scientific and philosophical field examines the nature of existence at the grandest scale — what is it called?
Cosmology (from Ancient Greek (cosmos) 'the universe, the world' and - (logia) 'study of') is the study of the nature of the universe, the cosmos.
Specialists in this branch of medicine handle skin infections, cancers, hair loss, and cosmetic concerns, sometimes even life-threatening conditions like severe burns — which medical field?
Dermatology is the branch of medicine dealing with the skin.
Sometimes triggered by lead poisoning or reactions to neuroleptic drugs, this neurological disorder produces involuntary, twisting muscle contractions — what is it?

Dystonia is a neurological hyperkinetic movement disorder in which sustained or repetitive muscle contractions occur involuntarily, resulting in twisting and repetitive movements or abnormal fixed postures.

Native only to a single island in French Polynesia, this arum-family plant is now one of the world's most popular houseplants, and an ecologically damaging invasive species from South Africa to the Pacific Islands. Name it?
Epipremnum aureum is a species in the arum family Araceae, native to Mo'orea in the Society Islands of French Polynesia.

Named for a physicist who reportedly asked 'But where is everybody?' over lunch in 1950, this puzzle contrasts the vast odds of alien civilizations with our total lack of evidence for them — what's it called?
Fermi paradox is the term for the apparent gap between the lack of conclusive evidence of extraterrestrial civilizations and the apparently high likelihood of their existence.
Son of a wealthy Greek architect, this 2nd-century physician and philosopher's writings shaped anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, and neurology for centuries after his death — who is he?
As emeritus chairman of the company he co-founded, this American engineer lent his name to a law predicting steady doubling of transistor counts on integrated circuits — who is he?
Gordon Moore (January 3, 1929 - March 24, 2023) was an American businessman, scientist, engineer, and the co-founder and emeritus chairman of Intel Corporation.
Tapeworms, flukes, and roundworms burrowing into the gut and beyond all fall under this macroparasitic disease — a neglected tropical illness better known as worm infection. What is it?
Helminthiasis is any macroparasitic disease of humans and other animals in which a part of the body is infected with parasitic worms, known as helminths.

Also called prussic acid, this highly toxic and flammable liquid boils just above room temperature at 25.6 degrees Celsius. It is produced industrially as a precursor to many chemical compounds, particularly potassium cyanide and adiponitrile. What is it?
Hydrogen cyanide (also called prussic acid) is a chemical compound with the formula HCN and structural formula HCN.
Its name comes from the Ancient Greek for 'violet,' fitting for an element that boils into a violet gas — and it sits at atomic number 53 as the heaviest stable halogen. What is it?
Iodine is a chemical element; it has symbol I and atomic number 53.
This English scientist's 1808 book proposed that elements consist of identical atoms combining in fixed whole-number ratios, laying the groundwork for modern atomic theory — who is he?
John Dalton (5 or 6 September 1766 - 27 July 1844) was an English chemist, physicist, and meteorologist whose work laid the foundations of modern atomic theory and stoichiometric chemistry.
This Arab dessert layers spun pastry dough with cheese, soaked in a sugar syrup, with its most famous variant hailing from the Palestinian city of Nablus — what is it?
Knafeh is a traditional Arab dessert made with kadayif (spun pastry dough) layered with cheese and soaked in a sweet, sugar-based syrup called attar.
This big-cat hybrid, born of a male lion and a female tiger, is the largest of all living cats, growing larger than either parent and enjoying a swim. What animal is it?
Liger is a hybrid offspring of a male lion (Panthera leo) and a tigress, or female tiger (Panthera tigris).

Developed by MathWorks, this proprietary programming language and numeric computing environment is built around matrix manipulation, and pairs with an add-on called Simulink for graphical simulation and model-based design. What software is this?
MATLAB (Matrix Laboratory) is a proprietary multi-paradigm programming language and numeric computing environment developed by MathWorks.
A German historian, jurist, and political economist born in 1864, he is counted among the central founders of sociology and still shapes social theory today — who was he?

Max Weber (21 April 1864 - 14 June 1920) was a German sociologist, historian, jurist, and political economist who was one of the central figures in the development of sociology and the social sciences more generally.
This unit of time, normally equal to 60 seconds, can rarely stretch to 61 seconds under the UTC time standard because of a leap second — what is it?
Minute (symbol: min) is a unit of time defined as equal to 60 seconds.

This European twin-engine military helicopter was the first production helicopter ever built with entirely fly-by-wire flight controls, coming in both troop-transport and naval anti-submarine variants — what aircraft is it?
NHIndustries NH90 is a medium-sized European twin-engine multi-role military helicopter.
Which Turkish-born American economist, an NYU Stern professor, earned lasting fame as one of the few who predicted the 2008 subprime mortgage crisis?
Nouriel Roubini (born March 29, 1958) is a Turkish-born American economic consultant, economist, speaker, and writer.
Also called trioxygen and far less stable than the oxygen we breathe, it carries the formula O3 and smells faintly of chlorine — what is this gas?
Ozone is an inorganic molecule with the chemical formula O3.
What medical term describes damage or disease affecting the nerves — impairing sensation, movement, gland, or organ function — commonly caused by systemic diseases such as diabetes?

Peripheral neuropathy is damage or disease affecting the nerves. Peripheral neuropathy may be acute (with sudden onset, rapid progress) or chronic (symptoms begin subtly and progress slowly), and may be reversible or permanent.
This zodiac sign's Latin name means 'fishes,' and it's where the ecliptic crosses the celestial equator near the March equinox — which one?
Pisces (constellation) is a constellation of the zodiac. It is between Aquarius, of similar size, to the southwest and Aries, which is smaller, to the east.
This Danish midfielder won three Eredivisie titles at Ajax before being twice named his London club's Player of the Year during a six-year spell there. Who is he?
Priapism is a condition in which a penis remains erect for hours in the absence of stimulation or after stimulation has ended.
It can form not just from rain but from mist, spray, or dew, and though we usually see an arc, it can actually be a full circle — what optical phenomenon is it?
Rainbow is an optical phenomenon caused by refraction, internal reflection and dispersion of light in water droplets resulting in a continuous spectrum of light appearing in the sky.
Known by the common name 'dog rose,' this climbing wild rose species is native across Europe and stretches into northwest Africa and western Asia — which species?
Rosa canina is a variable climbing, wild rose species native to Europe, northwest Africa, and western Asia.
Which leathery-skinned marine echinoderm, of which about 1,786 species are known worldwide, plays a vital ecological role on the sea floor by breaking down detritus as a scavenger?
Sea cucumber are echinoderms from the class Holothuroidea.
This group of nocturnal Southeast Asian primates ranges from Yunnan province in China down to the island of Java, with a pygmy relative recently reclassified into its own genus — what are they?
Slow loris are a group of several species of nocturnal strepsirrhine primates that make up the genus Nycticebus.
Innervated by the accessory nerve, which of the body's largest and most superficial neck structures rotates the head to the opposite side and flexes the neck?
Sternocleidomastoid muscle is one of the largest and most superficial cervical muscles.
This actress and singer's breakout role on Pretty Little Liars won her seven Teen Choice Awards, more than any actress in a single series. Who is she?
Tarragon (Artemisia dracunculus), also known as estragon, is a species of perennial herb in the family Asteraceae.
This intensely itchy, contagious fungal skin infection produces a red, scaly rash with a curved border across the groin and buttocks, mostly in men — what is it?

Tinea cruris (TC), also known as jock itch, is a common type of contagious, superficial fungal infection of the groin and buttocks region, which occurs predominantly but not exclusively in men and in hot-humid climates.
A byproduct of purine breakdown normally found in urine, elevated blood levels of this heterocyclic compound can cause gout and kidney stones — what's the compound (C5H4N4O3)?
Uric acid is a heterocyclic compound of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and hydrogen with the formula C5H4N4O3.
These big cetaceans — everything in the group except dolphins and porpoises — count the hippopotamus as their closest living relative on land. What are they?
Whale are a widely distributed and diverse group of fully aquatic placental marine mammals.

Unlike a user interface, which links a computer to a person, this software connection lets programs talk directly to each other — and the standard describing it is called its specification. What's the three-letter term?
API: Connection between computers or programs.
Nicknamed the 'killer' variety for its aggressive defense of the hive, this hybrid pollinating insect escaped Brazilian quarantine in 1957 and reached Texas by 1990 — which insect is it?
Africanized bee: Hybrid species of bee. The African honey bee was first introduced to Brazil in 1956 to increase honey production, but 26 swarms escaped quarantine in 1957.
Unlike its bulb-forming relative, the common onion, this perennial vegetable never forms a bulb and owes one of its names to its hollow, tube-like leaves — which plant?
Allium fistulosum: Species of plant. The species is very similar in taste and odor to the related common onion, Allium cepa, and hybrids between the two (tree onions) exist.
This Russian physicist miraculously survived a 1978 accident in which a high-energy proton beam from a particle accelerator passed directly through his skull — who is he?
Anatoli Bugorski: Soviet and Russian scientist (born 1942)
Lacking a tail due to a mutation in the TBXT gene, this superfamily of primates includes gibbons as the 'lesser' branch and humans among the 'great' branch — which animal group?
Ape: Superfamily of primates. The family Hylobatidae, the lesser apes, include four genera and a total of 20 species of gibbon, including the lar gibbon and the siamang, all native to Asia.
Born from acetylsalicylic acid, this everyday drug cools fevers within about 30 minutes and is taken long-term to fend off heart attacks and strokes by quieting platelets — what is it?
One of the first grains ever domesticated, around 9000 BC in the Fertile Crescent, this cereal now ranks fourth in world production — and 70% of it goes to feeding animals — what is it?
Barley: Cereal grain. Barley (Hordeum vulgare), a member of the grass family, is a major cereal grain grown in temperate climates globally.
This red-orange breakdown product of heme colors feces brown and urine pale yellow as it's further broken down in the body — which compound?
Bilirubin: Red pigment of the bile.
Named for a Native American people of Oregon and Washington, this tandem-rotor heavy-lift helicopter grew out of Vertol's 1957 Model 107 design — what aircraft is it?
Boeing CH-47 Chinook: American tandem-rotor helicopter introduced in 1962 during the Cold War.
This group of roughly 20,000 non-vascular land plant species — liverworts, hornworts, and mosses — reproduces by spores instead of flowers or seeds. What is it called?
Bryophyte: Terrestrial plants that lack vascular tissue.
Once used in Italy for hunting large game and herding cattle, this mastiff breed today mostly serves as a guard dog or companion — which breed?
Cane Corso: Italian breed of mastiff. It is usually kept as a companion dog or guard dog; it may also be used to protect livestock.
Marked by patients who may lie motionless for days or repeat purposeless movements, this neuropsychiatric syndrome often responds to benzodiazepines or electroconvulsive therapy — which condition?
Domesticated from the red junglefowl roughly 8,000 years ago, this bird now numbers over 26 billion worldwide, more than any other domesticated species — what is it?
Chicken: Domesticated subspecies of red junglefowl. The chicken (Gallus gallus domesticus) is the domesticated form of the red junglefowl (Gallus gallus), originally native to Southeast Asia.
Native to the Indonesian island that gave part of its scientific name, this legume flower also goes by butterfly pea or blue pea — what is it?
Its species name honors Colchis, an ancient region on the Black Sea, and it's often released into the wild as a game bird — which Asian-native, ring-necked bird is this?
Common pheasant: Species of bird. The common pheasant (Phasianus colchicus), ring-necked pheasant, or blue-headed pheasant, is a bird in the pheasant family (Phasianidae).
Broken down from creatine phosphate in muscle metabolism, this compound is released into the blood at a rate tied to a person's muscle mass — what is it?
Creatinine: Breakdown product of creatine phosphate.
Also called thornapple or devil's trumpet, this genus of nine highly poisonous nightshade plants lent its American name to an outbreak in colonial Jamestown — what genus is it?
Datura: Genus of poisonous, potentially psychoactive plants.

This colourless, water-mixable lab solvent is technically odorless — but degraded samples reek of fish thanks to a dimethylamine impurity. It's better known by a three-letter abbreviation; what's the compound?
Dimethylformamide: Chemical compound. Dimethylformamide, DMF is an organic compound with the chemical formula HCON(CH3)2.
This German-born British economist championed 'human-scale, appropriate technology' in his 1973 book, later ranked among the 100 most influential books since World War II — who was he?
E. F. Schumacher: British statistician and economist (1911–1977)
Derived from Greek words for 'brain' and 'suffering,' this umbrella medical term covers any disease or disorder that causes overall brain dysfunction — what is it?
Encephalopathy: Disorders or diseases of the brain.
Combining five of mathematics' most fundamental constants — e, i, pi, 1, and 0 — into a single elegant equation, this formula is often called the most beautiful in mathematics. What is it?
Euler's identity: Mathematical equation linking e, i and π.
Its 41 living species boast the most varied fur patterns of any land carnivore, all armed with retractile claws and an obligate taste for meat — which family is this?
Felidae: Family of mammals. Felidae ( FEE-lə-dee) is the family of mammals in the order Carnivora colloquially referred to as cats.

First described by 19th-century French psychiatrists Charles Lasègue and Jules Falret, this rare condition — also called shared psychotic disorder — lets one person's delusion spread to another. What is it called?

Folie à deux: Shared psychosis, a psychotic disorder. The disorder, first conceptualized in 19th century French psychiatry by Charles Lasègue and Jules Falret, is also known as Lasègue–Falret syndrome.
Also known as reishi or lingzhi, this red-colored fungus grows on decaying hardwood in parts of Europe and China — what is it?
Named from a Latin word for sword, this genus of cormous flowering plants in the iris family is sometimes called the 'sword lily' and is most diverse in South Africa's Cape region — which genus?
Gladiolus: Genus of perennial flowering plants. It is sometimes called the 'sword lily', but is usually called by its generic name (plural gladioli).
Designed specifically for airborne early warning rather than adapted from an existing airframe, this twin-turboprop carrier plane replaced the piston-engined Tracer for the US Navy — which aircraft?
Grumman E-2 Hawkeye: Airborne early warning and control aircraft. The Northrop Grumman E-2 Hawkeye is an American all-weather, carrier-capable, tactical airborne early warning (AEW) aircraft.
Nicknamed bindwood or lovestone, this clinging evergreen native to Europe scales tree trunks, walls, and fences — which plant?
Hedera helix: Species of flowering plant.
This genus of over 570 flowering plants — the only living genus in its family — includes the evergreen shrub famous for Christmas decorations and cards. What genus is it?
Holly: Genus of flowering plants. Ilex or holly is a genus of over 570 species of flowering plants in the family Aquifoliaceae, and the only living genus in that family.
This immune response causes tissue damage upon repeated exposure to an antigen and underlies conditions like hay fever, which affects roughly one in ten people worldwide — what is it called?
Hypersensitivity: Overreaction of the immune system to an antigen.
This sugar alcohol, with about half the sweetness of table sugar, is made by the human kidney at roughly two grams a day and reaches its highest concentration in the brain — what is it?
Inositol: Carbocyclic sugar. Its formula is C6H12O6; the molecule has a ring of six carbon atoms, each with a hydrogen atom and a hydroxy group (–OH).
Often mislabeled 'yellowtail tuna' on sushi menus, this northwest Pacific jack fish is unrelated to true tuna and is called hamachi when served as sashimi — which species?
Japanese amberjack: Species of fish. The Japanese amberjack or yellowtail, Seriola quinqueradiata, is a species of jack fish in the family Carangidae, native to the northwest Pacific Ocean.
Also known as the English or Persian walnut, this tree species native to Eurasia is cultivated worldwide, with China as its leading producer today — what is it?
Juglans regia: Species of tree (walnut). Juglans regia, known by various common names including the common walnut, English walnut, or Persian walnut amongst other names, is a species of walnut.
Caused by a thiamine deficiency often linked to heavy alcohol use, this brain disorder is marked by amnesia and confabulation, and frequently pairs with Wernicke encephalopathy — which condition?
Korsakoff syndrome: Mental illness caused by a lack of thiamine in the brain.
Distinguished by coloured scales, large triangular wings, and a nectar-sipping proboscis, which insect order encompasses both butterflies and moths?
Lepidoptera: Order of insects including moths and butterflies.
Based on the L-188 Electra airliner and distinguished by a tail 'stinger' used to magnetically detect submarines, this four-engine turboprop has served the US Navy since the 1960s — which aircraft?
Lockheed P-3 Orion: Maritime patrol and anti-submarine aircraft family.
Known historically as 'magnesia alba' to distinguish it from a manganese-containing mineral called 'magnesia nigra,' this white hygroscopic solid has the formula MgO — what is it?
Magnesium oxide: Chemical compound naturally occurring as periclase.
Among the first women in Canada to earn a medical doctorate, this physician-chemist is best known for her 1913 work with Leonor Michaelis on enzyme kinetics — who was she?
Maud Menten: Canadian physician and chemist (1879–1960)
Marketed under brand names like Quaalude and Sopor, this sedative was pulled from commercial production in the mid-1980s due to widespread misuse — which drug?
This synthetic prostaglandin medication treats stomach ulcers, induces labor, and — often paired with mifepristone — is used to end a pregnancy. What drug is it?
Misoprostol: Medication to induce abortion and treat ulcers.

Grouping over 30 inherited disorders that cause progressive weakening and wasting of skeletal tissue — with the Duchenne form affecting roughly half of all cases in young boys — what's this disease group called?
Muscular dystrophy: Diseases in which skeletal and visceral muscles break down over time.
A cable-like bundle of axons wrapped in three layers of connective tissue, this structure carries electrochemical signals called action potentials — what is it?
Nerve: Cable-like bundle of axons. The axons are bundled together into groups called fascicles, and each fascicle is wrapped in a layer of connective tissue called the perineurium.
Represented by symbols like '11' in the Hindu-Arabic system used worldwide, these mathematical objects serve to count, measure, and label — what are they called?
Number: Used to count, measure, and label. The most basic examples are the natural numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and so forth.
Nicknamed 'brittle bone disease,' this genetic disorder causes fragile bones and blue-tinted eye whites, usually stemming from faulty type I collagen — what is it?
Osteogenesis imperfecta: Group of genetic disorders resulting in fragile bones.

Also called the blue passionflower, this South American vine climbs via tendrils to 10 metres, bears fragrant blue-white blooms with a fringed coronal filament, and produces an edible but not particularly tasty orange fruit — which plant is it?
Passiflora caerulea: Species of flowering plant in the passion flower family.
This Belgian-British microbiologist helped discover the Ebola virus in 1976, fought to contain its first recorded outbreak, then became a pioneering AIDS researcher — who is he?

Cultivated for its edible nuts since prehistoric times and native to the Mediterranean and the Levant, this pine species has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit — which species?
Pinus pinea: Species of pine tree. Pinus pinea, the Italian stone pine or Mediterranean stone pine, is a tree from the pine family, Pinaceae.
Stockpiled for radiation emergencies, this oral compound floods and shields the thyroid gland — and also treats hyperthyroidism and the skin infection sporotrichosis. Which compound is it?
